title_es: Diseño de sistemas a gran escala
body_es:
Diseñar sistemas que sirvan a millones de usuarios requiere razonar sobre múltiples dimensiones simultáneamente: throughput (peticiones por segundo), latencia (tiempo de respuesta p99), disponibilidad (SLA de 99.9% = 8.7h de inactividad/año, 99.99% = 52 min/año), costes y operabilidad.

El proceso habitual empieza por establecer el volumen: ¿cuántos usuarios activos? ¿Qué tasa de escrituras frente a lecturas? Con esos números se calculan los requerimientos de almacenamiento y red. A continuación se define la arquitectura de alto nivel: qué bases de datos, qué capas de caché, cómo se particiona la carga.

Los principios aplicados consistentemente en sistemas de gran escala son: stateless services (fáciles de escalar horizontalmente), caching agresivo de datos calientes, particionado de datos (sharding) para distribuir la carga de escritura, CDN para assets estáticos, colas asíncronas para operaciones no críticas en latencia, y circuit breakers para aislar fallos.

Un ejercicio típico de diseño de sistema pide diseñar Twitter, Instagram o un sistema de URL shortening. La respuesta esperada incluye el back-of-the-envelope calculation, la decisión de base de datos, el esquema de caché y la estrategia de escalado.
body_en:
Designing systems that serve millions of users requires reasoning across multiple dimensions simultaneously: throughput (requests per second), tail latency (p99 response time), availability (99.9% SLA = 8.7 hours downtime per year; 99.99% = 52 minutes), cost, and operational complexity.

The process starts with estimations: how many daily active users? What is the read/write ratio? These numbers drive storage, bandwidth, and compute requirements. Next comes the high-level architecture: which databases, which cache layers, how to partition load.

Principles consistently applied in large-scale systems include: stateless services (trivially horizontally scalable), aggressive caching of hot data, data sharding to distribute write load, CDN for static assets, async queues for latency-insensitive operations, and circuit breakers to isolate failures.

Back-of-the-envelope calculation is a core skill: estimating that 100 million daily tweets at 280 bytes each requires roughly 26 GB/day of raw storage immediately narrows database choices and replication strategies. The example models a URL shortener's storage requirements.
example_code:
# Back-of-the-envelope: URL shortener capacity planning
DAILY_NEW_URLS       = 100_000_000   # 100M new shortened URLs per day
READ_WRITE_RATIO     = 100           # 100 reads per write
BYTES_PER_URL_RECORD = 500          # long URL + short code + metadata
RETENTION_YEARS      = 5

writes_per_second = DAILY_NEW_URLS // 86_400
reads_per_second  = writes_per_second * READ_WRITE_RATIO
total_records     = DAILY_NEW_URLS * 365 * RETENTION_YEARS
storage_tb        = (total_records * BYTES_PER_URL_RECORD) // (10 ** 12)
bandwidth_mbps    = (reads_per_second * BYTES_PER_URL_RECORD * 8) // 1_000_000

print(f'Writes/s       : {writes_per_second:>10,}')
print(f'Reads/s        : {reads_per_second:>10,}')
print(f'Total records  : {total_records:>10,}')
print(f'Storage needed : {storage_tb:>10,} TB over {RETENTION_YEARS} years')
print(f'Read bandwidth : {bandwidth_mbps:>10,} Mbps')
print()
print('Architecture decision: read-heavy -> aggressive caching + CDN')
print('Storage: 91 TB -> sharding needed (e.g. by short-code hash range)')
example_output:
Writes/s       :      1,157
Reads/s        :    115,700
Total records  : 182,500,000,000
Storage needed :         91 TB over 5 years
Read bandwidth :        462 Mbps

Architecture decision: read-heavy -> aggressive caching + CDN
Storage: 91 TB -> sharding needed (e.g. by short-code hash range)
source: System Design Interview — Alex Xu (ByteByteGo, 2020) — https://bytebytego.com/
